extracted.intended_audience: students, poets, dramatists, and literary critics (readers of classical poetics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for composing and judging poetry (especially tragedy and epic), covering mimesis, elements of tragedy, plot construction, character, diction, and practical rules for poets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation (mimesis) as the principle of the arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry and allied arts are modes of imitation; imitation is the common principle of the arts of poetry, music, dancing, painting, and sculpture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation may be produced through different media and modes; the poet imitates actions and life to reveal universal truths rather than mere particular facts. The account explains psychological (instinct of imitation, harmony and rhythm) and historical origins of poetry as background justification for the art. (Context: used to justify why poetic rules aim at representing the universal via imitation.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium of imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The medium of imitation is rhythm, language, and 'harmony' (or melody), taken singly or combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the appropriate medium (e.g., metre for epic, melody and chorus for tragedy) to suit the kind of imitation; the selection of medium affects the expressive possibilities and audience reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation (higher or lower types)
rubrics_metrics.description: The objects represented by imitation differ in dignity; higher or lower types are represented in the imitative arts and in poetry this distinguishes tragedy from comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the proper level/type of character and action for the genre: tragedy represents higher or noble forms, comedy lower or ridiculous types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner (mode) of imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry may be in form dramatic, narrative, or mixed (including lyric poetry); the manner of imitation (dramatic vs. narrative) is a primary distinguishing feature of genres like tragedy and epic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to use pure drama, pure narrative, or a blend (e.g., epic narrative with dramatic episodes) depending on the desired scope, unity, and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six constituent elements of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy has six elements: Spectacular Presentment (spectacle), Lyrical Song (chorus/melody), Diction (language), Plot (mythos), Character (ethos), and Thought (dianoia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot is primary; character and thought are next in importance; spectacle and chorus are external but significant. Evaluate a tragedy first by the quality of its plot, then character and thought, and finally by diction, melody, and spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot (the representation of the action) is of primary importance in tragedy; everything should serve the plot as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good poem's plot must be the organizing principle — incidents, character, diction, and chorus must contribute to the plot's unity and end. Example anti-pattern: incidents introduced only for spectacular effect rather than serving causal sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot must be a Whole (completeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot must be a Whole, complete in itself, and of adequate magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plot must have a beginning, middle, and end; it should form an organic whole such that removing or changing parts disturbs its integrity. Scoring note: completeness and self-sufficiency are key criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (unity of plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of Plot consists in unity of action, not unity of the hero; the incidents must be necessary/probable consequences of one another and form one complete action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid episodic or unconnected subplots; judge unity by causal or probable sequence. Anti-pattern: multiple independent actions shoehorned into one work, or adding incidents that don't follow from prior events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude / Appropriate length
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot must be of adequate magnitude — neither too short to achieve the intended effect nor so long that its unity is lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy achieves concentrated effect within limited time; epic permits broader length. Compare forms: a tragic concentration of a large subject dilutes effect if stretched to epic length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of probable or necessary sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidents in a poem should follow by probability or necessity; dramatic truth (universal) should govern sequencing rather than mere historical particularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use necessity or convincing probability to bind events; prefer probable impossibility (an imaginative but coherent construction) to mere improbable possibility that undermines belief. Evaluate causal plausibility rather than strict factual realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of plot: Simple vs Complex
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple plots are continuous without reversal/recognition; complex plots include reversal (peripeteia), recognition (anagnorisis), and suffering (pathos).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex plots that effect a reversal and recognition are more powerful for producing tragic emotions; identify presence, placement, and organic integration of these devices. Examples and definitions are provided in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal (peripeteia), Recognition (anagnorisis), and Pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal is a change to the opposite in the course of events; recognition is a change from ignorance to knowledge; pathos is a scene of suffering or destructive incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All three are mechanisms to produce pity and fear when they arise inevitably from the plot. Evaluate whether reversals and recognitions are plausible and necessary, and whether pathos arises from the action rather than spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic emotions should spring from the Plot (pity and fear)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic emotions of pity and fear should arise naturally from the plot itself, not from scenery or spectacular effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: manufacturing pity/fear by spectacle or sensational staging. Good practice: structure events and recognitions so the audience experiences pity and fear through understanding the necessary/probable outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (ethical portraiture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character is the manifestation of moral purpose; requisites include consistency, appropriateness to the plot, and idealization where suitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should be believable, show moral purpose through action, and be fitted to the plot's exigencies. A tragic hero should be neither wholly good nor villainous but of a kind that makes reversal/recognition plausible. Evaluate for ethical plausibility and fit to action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (dianoia) as the intellectual element
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought consists of the intellectual content of speeches — the themes, arguments, and inferences — and is expressed according to rules of rhetoric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess speeches for clarity, argumentative force, and suitability to character and situation. Thought reveals goals and reasoning and should align with the plot's logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (language) and Poetic Diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction or language in poetry covers choice of words, metaphor, and modes of speech admissible in poetry; it combines elevation with perspicuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate words and figures (especially metaphor) to suit genre and character; avoid obscure or overwrought language. Poetic diction should be elevated but clear; evaluate appropriateness of style to the subject and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melody/Chorus and Spectacle (external elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody (lyrical song/chorus) and Spectacle (stage presentation) are external elements of tragedy; the chorus should be an organic part of the whole, spectacle is least artistic but may produce vivid pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate choral odes organically into the plot; do not rely on spectacle to produce the essential tragic effects. Spectacle can enhance but should not substitute for plot-driven emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical craft rules for the tragic poet
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical precepts: (1) place the scene before his eyes and act the parts to enter into sympathy with the dramatis personae; (2) sketch the outline of action before filling in episodes; plus further rules about complication and denouement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should visualize and rehearse to achieve vividness; plan the action's skeleton to maintain unity; be careful with complication and especially with the dénouement to preserve plausibility. Make episodes serve the plot and avoid unnecessary diversions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compositional 'quantitative parts' and their proper use
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is composed of parts such as Prologue, Episodes, Choral Odes, etc.; each has its role and proper placement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use each part for its function (e.g., prologue to set up action, episodes to carry it forward, choral odes to reflect and heighten) and ensure they contribute to the unity and magnitude of the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic vs Tragedy: comparative criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic and Tragedy share unity of action but differ in length, metre, narrative mode, and the art of imparting plausibility to fiction; tragedy attains a concentrated effect and is judged superior in attaining its end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a work's mode (narrative vs dramatic), length, and unity suit its aims; a concentrated dramatic treatment produces more vivid and unified pleasure than diffusely long epic treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth vs Historical truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry expresses the universal (what may happen, what is typical), while history records the particular (what actually happened); dramatic unity and probability are judged by poetic truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a poem by whether it embodies universal plausibility and necessary sequence rather than strict historical accuracy. The poet may rightly deviate from facts to better represent universal truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable departures from realism (probable impossibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: In terms of artistic correctness, a probable impossibility (an imaginative but coherent construction) is preferable to something merely possible but improbable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowed anti-realistic devices must preserve coherence and poetic truth; judges should prefer bold but internally consistent inventions over unlikely but disjointed events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling critical objections to poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Five sources of criticism: a poem may be censured as impossible, irrational, morally hurtful, contradictory, or contrary to artistic correctness; answers should be sought under the twelve heads treated earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defending a work, show how it satisfies the elements (plot, character, thought, diction, melody, spectacle) and conforms to poetic truth; identify whether objections attack factuality, morality, or artistic form and respond by reference to unity, probability, and poetic function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for Recognition scenes and their kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition (change from ignorance to knowledge) has various kinds and must arise naturally from the action; it must be plausibly set up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether recognitions are prepared by earlier hints or evidence and whether they cohere with characters' knowledge and the plot's causal sequence; avoid sudden, unmotivated disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choral Odes must be organic
rubrics_metrics.description: The choral odes should be made like an organic part of the whole, contributing to, not interrupting, the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure chorus content and placement support themes, reflect action, and aid unity rather than serve as decorative digressions.
